screens.title: Writing Assembly Programs: Loops, Conditionals, and I/O
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we learn how to express control flow and simple input/output using only the Hack machine's primitive operations: loads, stores, ALU calculations, and unconditional or conditional jumps. You will see how loops become labeled cycles that check a counter, how conditionals are implemented by computing a comparison and jumping around blocks of code, and how the memory-mapped screen and keyboard give you very direct input and output control. We'll also examine how subroutines require the programmer to manage return addresses manually, and how the C P U Emulator helps you step through instructions, inspect registers, and find off-by-one and logic errors. Practical examples include counting loops, a compare-and-select conditional, drawing a filled rectangle by iterating over screen addresses, reading the keyboard as a single memory read, and implementing multiplication by repeated addition. By the end you'll know not only the mechanics of these patterns but debugging techniques and small programs to test them. Think of assembly as a puzzle: you have a tiny instruction set and you must compose those pieces to build common high-level constructs. Which low-level choice will you try first when converting a simple for-loop into labels and jumps?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Introduction
Writing Assembly Programs
Learn loops, conditionals, subroutines, and memory-mapped I/O in Hack assembly.
Orientation

You will convert high-level control structures into labels, explicit jump checks, and register/memory operations. The chapter shows canonical patterns and debugging steps.

In this lesson
Patterns for loops and conditionals, memory-mapped screen and keyboard I/O, subroutine call patterns, and CPU Emulator debugging practices.
Explore Key Topics
Loops
Label + conditional jump create iterative loops and countdowns.
I/O
Screen writes and keyboard reads use specific RAM addresses for memory-mapped I/O.
Debugging
The CPU Emulator lets you step, inspect registers and set breakpoints to validate loop behavior.
Visual Concept
Assembly Patterns
Init: set counters, addresses
Loop: label + conditional jump
I/O: write to SCREEN, read KBD
Return: save and restore return address
This static concept visual groups the common assembly steps you will apply across examples and lab tasks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson prepares you to reason at the machine level. First, you'll learn to write Hack assembly programs using explicit loops, conditionals, and, when necessary, subroutines. That skill matters because it forces you to manage state and control flow with precision, which improves debugging and teaches how high-level constructs are compiled. Second, you'll implement input and output by writing to the screen memory map and reading the keyboard memory address. Direct input and output is the only way to communicate with users on the Hack platform. Third, you'll understand the manual calling convention for subroutines: how return addresses are stored and restored. This clarifies how higher-level function calls work under the hood. Finally, you will use the C P U Emulator to debug by stepping, setting breakpoints, and watching memory. Debugging at the instruction level teaches you to validate each loop iteration and check boundary conditions. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a concrete reason you will use it during programming and testing.

For input and output, the milestone is a keyboard-echo program that reads the keyboard memory address and updates the display in real time, showing you can read and present user input. For subroutines, your milestone is to implement a call/return pattern using the stack to save a return address, which trains you to manage control flow across code sections. For debugging, the milestone is to use the C P U Emulator to find and fix an off-by-one loop error by stepping through the jump instruction and watching the counter. Each milestone pairs a small program with verification steps so you can prove competency and understand where errors commonly arise.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Applied Milestones
01 — Factorial in assembly
Write an assembly program that computes n! for small n and stores the result in RAM[0]. Verify each iteration and boundary conditions.
Success check
  • Walk the first two iterations by hand.
  • Set breakpoints at loop entry and verify the counter update.
02 — Keyboard echo
Continuously read the keyboard memory address and display the ASCII code or character on the screen. Test by pressing keys and observing the update.
Success check
  • Confirm D=M at keyboard returns zero when idle.
  • Ensure screen writes refresh after each key press.
03 — Subroutine convention
Implement a caller that stores a return address on a software stack, jumps to a routine, and restores the return address to return correctly.
Success check
  • Trace call and return addresses in memory.
  • Confirm program counter returns to caller after the routine ends.
04 — Debug an off-by-one
Use the CPU Emulator to find why a loop runs one extra time by stepping to the conditional jump and inspecting the counter and its updates.
Success check
  • Break at the jump and inspect the counter value each iteration.
  • Try moving the decrement before or after the check to observe effects.

screens.title: Loops in Hack Assembly
screens.narratorSegment: A loop in Hack assembly is the explicit construction of an iterative cycle using labels and jumps. You initialize a counter in memory or a register, label the loop entry point, check the counter with an ALU operation, conditionally jump to exit when the stop condition is met, update the counter, then unconditionally jump back to the loop label. A canonical countdown example initializes R A M[counter] to ten and then decrements until zero. The important distinction from high-level languages is that there is no implicit loop frame: you must decide whether to check before or after the body. That choice creates common off-by-one behaviors. For example, checking the counter at the start prevents an extra iteration, while checking at the end will execute the body at least once. When you write a loop, name the label clearly, initialize the counter in a separate step, and use the C P U Emulator to step the first few iterations. Concrete example: a countdown from 10 to 0 uses @10, D=A, @counter, M=D, a loop label, a read of @counter into D, a conditional D;JEQ to exit, a decrement of counter, and an unconditional 0;JMP back. Misconception: you cannot rely on the PC to roll over; explicit jumps are required. Key takeaway: decide entry or exit test intentionally and verify the counter update order in the C P U Emulator.

keyIdea.title: Loop Pattern
keyIdea.text: Initialize, label, test with conditional jump, update, and unconditional jump back; watch for off-by-one by checking when decrement occurs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Loops
Core Concept
Countdown loop example
This code initializes a counter and loops until it reaches zero.
@10
D=A
@counter
M=D

(LOOP)
@counter
D=M
@END
D;JEQ    // If counter == 0, jump to END

@counter
D=M-1
M=D
@LOOP
0;JMP    // Unconditional jump back to LOOP

(END)
@END
0;JMP    // Infinite loop at END
How it works
  • Initialize counter in RAM with an A-instruction and M=D store.
  • At LOOP read counter into D and jump to END when equal to zero.
  • Decrement then unconditionally jump back to continue iterating.
Concrete example
Use this pattern to count down seconds, iterate over memory addresses for screen drawing, or implement repeated addition for multiplication.
Key Takeaway

Position your conditional check deliberately: before the body to avoid extra iterations, or after to guarantee one execution.

Common mistake
Decrementing after the jump check can yield an extra iteration. Step the first two loops in the CPU Emulator to verify.

screens.title: Conditionals via Conditional Jumps
screens.narratorSegment: Conditionals in Hack assembly are implemented by computing a comparison into the D register and using conditional jump instructions to skip or execute code blocks. The canonical example compares x and y by loading x into D, subtracting y, and testing the sign of D. If D is greater than zero, the program jumps to the true branch; otherwise the code falls through to the else branch. The assembly relies on the ALU to compute x minus y and the jump instructions like JGT or JEQ to inspect the result. In concrete terms, you load @x, D=M, then @y, D=D-M; if you want to execute the true branch on x > y, use D;JGT to jump to IF_TRUE. The else branch is the next instructions that store y into z, followed by an unconditional jump to END. A misconception is to assume equality and greater-than checks use the same jump—each jump condition is distinct and must match your intended logic. Practice by translating simple high-level conditionals to sequences of load, ALU, conditional jump, and store. Debug by stepping to the comparison and verifying D's numeric value before the jump. Which jump condition best captures your intended test?

keyIdea.title: Conditional Pattern
keyIdea.text: Compute comparison in D, use the appropriate jump (JGT, JEQ, JLT), and structure branches with labels and an unconditional jump to skip alternate code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Conditionals
Definition
If x > y then z = x else z = y
Translate comparisons into ALU results and use conditional jumps to route execution.
@x
D=M
@y
D=D-M   // D = x - y
@IF_TRUE
D;JGT   // If x > y, jump to IF_TRUE

@y      // else: z = y
D=M
@z
M=D
@END
0;JMP

(IF_TRUE)
@x      // z = x
D=M
@z
M=D

(END)
@END
0;JMP
Explanation
  • Compute x minus y in D. Sign of D determines comparison result.
  • Use D;JGT to jump when x is greater; otherwise fall through to else code.
  • After executing one branch, unconditionally jump to END to avoid executing the other branch.
Concrete example
Use this pattern to choose a maximum value, to clamp results, or to route input handling depending on a key code range.
Pro tip

Write small unit tests: set known values for x and y, step to the compare, and confirm the jump decision matches the expected relation.

screens.title: Screen I/O — Writing Pixels to the SCREEN
screens.narratorSegment: Screen output on the Hack platform is achieved by writing values directly to the SCREEN memory map. The screen occupies a contiguous range of memory words; writing 0xFFFF to an address paints all pixels for that word. The standard pattern initializes an address pointer with the base SCREEN address, initializes a counter for how many words to write, then loops: check counter, write 0xFFFF to the current address, increment the address, decrement the counter, and repeat until finished. This pattern is useful for filling rectangles, clearing the screen, or painting repeated patterns. The rectangle example in the chapter shows how to prepare an address variable, a remaining-word counter, and a loop which sets M=-1 at each address. Important practical notes: compute the correct number of words for your region, and ensure the address pointer increments correctly to avoid off-by-one or writing outside the screen range. Debugging tip: use the emulator memory viewer to watch the range of SCREEN addresses while your program runs, and set a breakpoint when the counter reaches small values to confirm behavior. The key idea is that drawing is simply memory writes repeated under program control.

keyIdea.title: Screen Write Loop
keyIdea.text: Set SCREEN base into an address variable, loop writing 0xFFFF while decrementing a counter, and increment the address pointer each iteration.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Screen I/O
Process Flow
Fill a block of screen memory
Prepare an address pointer and a counter, then loop until the counter reaches zero.
@SCREEN
D=A
@addr
M=D

@8192   // 8K words = full screen
D=A
@n
M=D

(LOOP)
@n
D=M
@END
D;JEQ

@addr
A=M
M=-1    // 0xFFFF = all black pixels

@addr
M=M+1

@n
M=M-1
@LOOP
0;JMP

(END)
@END
0;JMP
Key steps
  1. Load SCREEN base into a pointer variable.
  2. Set the number of words to write into a counter.
  3. Loop: write 0xFFFF, increment pointer, decrement counter, conditionally exit.
Key Takeaway

Treat drawing as repeated, indexed memory writes. Validate your address range before large writes to avoid unintended memory modification.

Debug tip
In the CPU Emulator watch the SCREEN memory addresses you write to and set a breakpoint when the counter equals a small value to inspect address increments.

screens.title: Keyboard I/O — Reading Key Presses
screens.narratorSegment: Reading the keyboard in Hack assembly is unusually simple: a single memory read from the keyboard address returns the ASCII code of the pressed key, or zero if no key is pressed. This makes polling loops straightforward: read the keyboard memory, test whether the value is zero, and react when it becomes nonzero. A common pattern is a tight loop that repeatedly executes @KBD, D=M and then branches depending on whether D is zero. You can then move the ASCII code to a screen register or use it in logic. A concrete program is a keyboard echo: repeatedly read KBD and write the ASCII code or an interpreted character to the screen memory so the display updates in real time as keys are pressed. Be cautious about busy-wait loops: they consume C P U cycles and block other logic; consider adding simple state checks or debouncing logic. In the C P U Emulator, press keys while running the program and watch D change from zero to the ASCII value. A common misconception is thinking keyboard reads produce character strings; they return a single code per read, and your program must decide how to display or buffer characters.

keyIdea.title: Keyboard Read
keyIdea.text: Use @KBD followed by D=M to obtain a single ASCII code; test for zero to detect presence of a key press.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Keyboard I/O
Definition
Read a key with a single memory access
Use @KBD and D=M to poll for a key press. Nonzero D means a key was pressed.
Polling snippet
@KBD
D=M     // D = ASCII code of pressed key (0 if none)
Use case — Keyboard echo
Continuously read KBD; when D is nonzero, write the code to the screen buffer or convert it to a displayed symbol. Test by pressing keys while stepping the emulator.
Misconception

Keyboard reads do not return strings. They deliver a single code per read and your program must assemble sequences if you need full input lines.

Practical check
In the CPU Emulator watch the KBD memory address as you press keys; verify D becomes the expected ASCII code before you write it out.

screens.title: Subroutines and Return Addresses
screens.narratorSegment: Subroutines in Hack assembly require manual management of the return address because there is no hardware call stack or automatic return mechanism. The caller is responsible for saving the return address and the callee must transfer control back to that saved address. A common software convention is to use a memory-based stack: the caller pushes the return address onto the stack, pushes any required arguments, and then jumps to the subroutine label. The subroutine runs, places its result in agreed-upon locations, pops any local values if needed, retrieves the saved return address, and jumps to it. In this chapter we do not implement a full stack mechanism, but the concept is critical: without saving the return address either by storing PC in memory or using a software stack, you cannot return reliably. A concrete way to practice is to implement a single-call routine where the caller stores the address of the next instruction into a known R A M location, jumps to the subroutine, and the subroutine jumps back to that saved address. Misconception: assuming a simple jump and then returning by another jump without a saved address will overwrite control flow. Key takeaway: always save the return point before transferring control to a subroutine.

keyIdea.title: Manual Call/Return
keyIdea.text: Save the return address in memory (or on a software stack) before jumping to a subroutine; restore it to return correctly.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Subroutines
Architecture
Call and return without hardware support
Use a saved return address or a software stack to preserve the caller's continuation point before jumping to the subroutine.
Caller pattern (conceptual)
  1. Store address of next instruction into a RAM slot or push it to a stack.
  2. Jump to subroutine label.
  3. After return, continue execution from saved address.
Concrete practice
Implement a single call: have the caller write the next instruction address to RAM[savedReturn], jump to DO_WORK, and at the end of DO_WORK jump to the address stored in RAM[savedReturn]. Verify in the emulator that the PC returns as expected.
Misconception

Do not assume the PC auto-restores. Without a saved address, returns cannot resume at the caller's next instruction.

Why it matters
Understanding manual calls prepares you for the VM module where an abstract stack will formalize this pattern and support nested calls and local frames.

screens.title: Debugging with the CPU Emulator
screens.narratorSegment: The C P U Emulator is the primary tool for debugging Hack assembly. It lets you load an assembled program and step through instructions one at a time, inspect the PC, A and D registers, and view memory contents at any address. Use breakpoints to pause at crucial instructions, such as the conditional jump in a loop, and watch how register values and memory change across iterations. Effective debugging starts with small test cases that exercise a single loop or branch, then expands coverage. Useful techniques include tracing the first few loop iterations by hand while stepping the emulator, watching boundary values like zero and negative numbers, and monitoring memory locations used for counters and addresses. When a loop behaves incorrectly, set a breakpoint at the loop label and observe the counter before and after the decrement. For off-by-one bugs, move the decrement before the conditional check or after it to see the difference. The emulator also supports watching memory addresses so you can detect accidental writes outside intended regions. Key takeaway: combine stepping with directed tests to isolate the instruction that violates your intent.

keyIdea.text: Step instructions, set breakpoints at control checks, and watch memory and registers to locate logic and boundary errors.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Debugging
Process
Find logic errors with targeted stepping
Work with small test cases, step instructions, set breakpoints, and watch the values that matter.
Step-by-step
  1. Run first few instructions to warm state.
  2. Set breakpoint at loop entry or conditional jump.
  3. Step and watch counter and PC at each iteration.
Watch list
  • Registers: A, D, PC
  • Memory: counter, address pointer, SCREEN range
Key Takeaway

Combine small test inputs with breakpoints at control checks to quickly isolate incorrect instructions or data updates.

Common pitfall
Watching only high-level symptoms without stepping can miss the exact instruction where a register or memory location is wrong.

screens.title: Off-by-One Errors — Diagnosis and Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Off-by-one errors are pervasive in assembly because you explicitly control when the counter is checked and when it is updated. If you see a loop intended to run ten times executing eleven, the most likely culprits are the position of the decrement relative to the conditional check, an incorrect initial counter value, or the wrong jump condition. Diagnosis begins by setting a breakpoint at the conditional jump and observing the counter value each time the code reaches that instruction. If the counter reads ten at the first check and you expect nine, your initialization is off. If the counter is decremented after the jump check, the loop body will run once more than intended. Another common mistake is using a jump that allows equality when you intended strict inequality. To fix the bug, either change the order—decrement before checking—or adjust initialization by subtracting one at start, or switch to a different jump condition. A practical debugging strategy is to step the first two iterations by hand and record the counter values, then generalize the fix. Remember: in assembly there is no implicit loop semantics; the programmer must decide where to place checks and updates. Ask yourself which iteration values you expect when entering the conditional check; that expectation guides your correction.

To fix the bug, either change the order—decrement before checking—or adjust initialization by subtracting one at start, or switch to a different jump condition. A practical debugging strategy is to step the first two iterations by hand and record the counter values, then generalize the fix. Remember: in assembly there is no implicit loop semantics; the programmer must decide where to place checks and updates. Ask yourself which iteration values you expect when entering the conditional check; that expectation guides your correction.

keyIdea.title: Off-by-one Root Causes
keyIdea.text: Check initialization, update order, and jump condition; use the emulator to trace the counter at each conditional jump.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Off-by-One
Comparison
Common causes and fixes
Compare initialization, decrement timing, and the jump condition to locate the off-by-one fault.
Checklist to debug
  • Verify initial counter value matches iteration count intent.
  • Inspect whether decrement happens before or after the conditional check.
  • Confirm the jump type (JGT, JGE, JEQ) matches desired logic.
Concrete debugging step
Set a breakpoint at the jump instruction. Step until the breakpoint and record the counter value on each hit. If the counter reaches the terminal value one iteration later than expected, move the decrement or adjust initialization accordingly.
Mistake to avoid

Avoid guessing. Use concrete recorded values from the emulator to choose the correct fix, not intuition alone.

screens.title: Multiplication by Repeated Addition
screens.narratorSegment: The Hack instruction set lacks hardware multiply, so multiplication is implemented in software by repeated addition. The algorithm sets a result variable to zero, copies the multiplicand and multiplier into working variables, then loops: if the multiplier is zero the routine ends; otherwise add the multiplicand to result, decrement multiplier, and repeat. This algorithm is O(n) in the value of the multiplier and is adequate for small numbers used in examples. The chapter provides a canonical assembly routine that moves R A M[0] into a named variable a, R A M[1] into b, initializes result to zero, then loops until b is zero. When finished it writes the result back into R A M[2]. Important points: ensure you copy values into working R A M locations to avoid destructive updates and verify the loop counter decrements properly. A misconception is assuming this is efficient for large operands—it's not, but it is simple and correct for small test cases. Use the C P U Emulator to step through a multiplication of small numbers such as 3 times 4 and verify the result increments correctly four times. This pattern also generalizes to other repeated-accumulate problems such as computing sums or dot products at the assembly level.

keyIdea.title: Software Multiply
keyIdea.text: Repeatedly add one operand into a result while decrementing the other operand until it reaches zero; store final result in a destination register.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Multiplication
Core Concept
Multiply via repeated addition
Copy operands to working RAM, loop adding multiplicand into result while decrementing multiplier.
@R0
D=M
@a
M=D
@R1
D=M
@b
M=D
@result
M=0

(LOOP)
@b
D=M
@END
D;JEQ    // If b == 0, done

@a
D=M
@result
M=M+D    // result = result + a

@b
M=M-1    // b = b - 1
@LOOP
0;JMP

(END)
@result
D=M
@R2
M=D
Complexity
This algorithm is linear in the multiplier value. For small inputs it is simple and reliable; for large inputs it is slow.
Practical tip

Test with small numbers like 3 and 4, step through the loop, and confirm result increments match the multiplier count.

Analogy
Think of multiplication as adding a pile repeatedly: you add the same pile as many times as the multiplier says.

screens.title: Activity: Fill Screen with Checkerboard Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to fill the screen with a checkerboard pattern. The approach is to iterate over the SCREEN memory map word by word, deciding whether to write all ones or all zeros for a given word depending on its row or column parity. One practical strategy is to compute the row index for each address and use a small conditional: if row is even write 0xFFFF for alternating words, otherwise write 0x0000 or the inverse pattern. Implementation steps: initialize an address pointer to SCREEN, set a counter for the number of words you will process, and set up a simple parity calculation using a small counter that toggles every word or every row. In assembly you will use labels, conditional jumps, and stores to implement the toggle. Test in small blocks first — for example, write only the first 32 words and inspect the emulator's screen memory to confirm the pattern. A common mistake is miscomputing the mapping between screen coordinates and word addresses; verify address increments correspond to pixel blocks you intend to flip. After success, extend to the full 8192 words. This exercise forces you to combine loop control, memory writes, and a small conditional to produce a visual result.

keyIdea.text: Iterate the screen addresses, compute parity for each word or row, and write 0xFFFF or 0x0000 accordingly to create the pattern.

Activity
Fill screen with a checkerboard pattern
Use parity toggles while iterating over the SCREEN address range to alternate words or rows.
Implementation steps
  1. Set pointer = SCREEN and words = small test count (e.g., 32).
  2. Use a parity variable that toggles each word or each row.
  3. In the loop write M = -1 when parity true, otherwise M = 0, then increment pointer and toggle parity.
  4. Test visually in the CPU Emulator and expand to full screen when correct.

Start small, verify address-to-pixel mapping, then scale to the full screen.

If the pattern looks shifted, re-check how your parity toggles across row boundaries and whether you increment the address exactly one word per step.

screens.title: Activity: Keyboard Echo and Interactive Display
screens.narratorSegment: The keyboard echo activity aims to continuously read the keyboard memory address and update a location on the screen with the ASCII code or a small visual representation. Implement a tight loop that polls @KBD, stores D=M, and branches if D is zero to continue waiting. When D is nonzero, write the code or a converted pixel representation to a predetermined screen address and then continue polling. Important considerations include clearing the previous display value if you want only the current key shown, and deciding whether to busy-wait or implement a simple debounce period. In the C P U Emulator you can press keys and observe the KBD memory change to nonzero and then the screen memory update immediately after. Test incrementally: first confirm that D=M reads nonzero when a key is pressed, then wire a single write to SCREEN and verify the expected memory word changes. A common mistake is assuming keyboard reads produce continuous streams; you must poll repeatedly and decide how to buffer or display sequences. This lab reinforces how a simple memory read connects directly to visible output with only a few assembly instructions.

keyIdea.title: Echo Loop
keyIdea.text: Poll @KBD repeatedly; when D is nonzero write to a fixed SCREEN address and continue polling to update in real time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Keyboard Echo
Activity
Create an interactive keyboard echo
Poll the keyboard memory and write the ASCII code or a symbol to the screen when a key is pressed.
@KBD
D=M
@NO_KEY
D;JEQ

// If nonzero, write D to a SCREEN address or map it to pixels
// Then continue polling
Test plan
  • Run program and press a key; confirm D becomes nonzero in the emulator.
  • Verify the target SCREEN memory cell updates immediately after the read.
  • Handle idle state by writing a blank or leaving previous value depending on expected UI.
Key Takeaway

Keyboard polling plus direct screen writes creates immediate interactivity with minimal instructions; design how you display single codes versus streams.

screens.title: Common Assembly Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Assembly programming relies on a small set of recurring patterns. Recognizing and composing these patterns reduces errors. The patterns are: initialization, where you set counters and pointers into memory; the loop body, which performs the work for each iteration; conditional checks that decide whether to continue or branch; and input and output actions that write to SCREEN or read KBD. Treat these as modular pieces: a program usually starts by initializing variables, then enters a loop that performs a conditional check, executes a body that may include input and output, updates state, and jumps back. Another common grouping is helper code: small subroutines that perform repeated tasks such as writing a single word to SCREEN or copying memory. In practice, keep each piece short so you can test it independently in the C P U Emulator. For example, verify your initialization alone by stepping to the first loop entry, then test the loop body with a single iteration, then validate the conditional logic. A common misconception is trying to write everything at once; instead, build and verify small pieces and combine them. Key takeaway: a reliable program comes from composing small, testable patterns and verifying each with the emulator.

Perform the core operation each iteration: add, write to screen, copy, or test conditions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Assembly programming composes high-level operations using a small set of primitives: loads and stores, ALU operations, labels, and jumps. Loops are labels plus a conditional check and an update. Conditionals compute comparisons and use specific jump instructions to pick branches. Screen input and output is achieved by writing words to the SCREEN memory range; keyboard input is a single memory read that yields the ASCII code or zero. Create loops and branches using labels and conditional or unconditional jumps.

Write to SCREEN to draw; read KBD to get the ASCII code of a pressed key.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: Keep a short checklist when writing and testing assembly programs. First, initialize all variables and pointers explicitly. Second, choose whether your loop tests before or after the body and ensure the counter update matches that decision. Third, when implementing conditionals pick the precise jump instruction—equality, greater-than or less-than—and compute the ALU result accordingly. Fourth, for input and output remember SCREEN writes are memory writes and keyboard reads are single-code memory reads. Finally, always use the C P U Emulator to step through failing code and inspect the registers and memory cells involved in the bug. These small rules-of-thumb reduce errors and make debugging faster. As you practice, these heuristics will become habits that speed your development of correct low-level programs. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we learn how to express control flow and simple input/output using only the Hack machine's primitive operations: loads, stores, ALU calculations, and unconditional or conditional jumps. You will see how loops become labeled cycles that check a counter, how conditionals are implemented by computing a comparison and jumping around blocks of code, and how the memory-mapped screen and keyboard give you very direct input and output control. We'll also examine how subroutines require the programmer to manage return addresses manually, and how the C P U Emulator helps you step through instructions, inspect registers, and find off-by-one and logic errors. Practical examples include counting loops, a compare-and-select conditional, drawing a filled rectangle by iterating over screen addresses, reading the keyboard as a single memory read, and implementing multiplication by repeated addition. By the end you'll know not only the mechanics of these patterns but debugging techniques and small programs to test them. Think of assembly as a puzzle: you have a tiny instruction set and you must compose those pieces to build common high-level constructs. Which low-level choice will you try first when converting a simple for-loop into labels and jumps?

This lesson prepares you to reason at the machine level. First, you'll learn to write Hack assembly programs using explicit loops, conditionals, and, when necessary, subroutines. That skill matters because it forces you to manage state and control flow with precision, which improves debugging and teaches how high-level constructs are compiled. Second, you'll implement input and output by writing to the screen memory map and reading the keyboard memory address. Direct input and output is the only way to communicate with users on the Hack platform. Third, you'll understand the manual calling convention for subroutines: how return addresses are stored and restored. This clarifies how higher-level function calls work under the hood. Finally, you will use the C P U Emulator to debug by stepping, setting breakpoints, and watching memory. Debugging at the instruction level teaches you to validate each loop iteration and check boundary conditions. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a concrete reason you will use it during programming and testing.

This follow-up objective screen connects each skill to a concrete milestone. For loops and conditionals, the milestone is to write an assembly routine that computes a factorial and stores the answer in R A M[0], proving you can manage counters, loop exits, and arithmetic. For input and output, the milestone is a keyboard-echo program that reads the keyboard memory address and updates the display in real time, showing you can read and present user input. For subroutines, your milestone is to implement a call/return pattern using the stack to save a return address, which trains you to manage control flow across code sections. For debugging, the milestone is to use the C P U Emulator to find and fix an off-by-one loop error by stepping through the jump instruction and watching the counter. Each milestone pairs a small program with verification steps so you can prove competency and understand where errors commonly arise.

A loop in Hack assembly is the explicit construction of an iterative cycle using labels and jumps. You initialize a counter in memory or a register, label the loop entry point, check the counter with an ALU operation, conditionally jump to exit when the stop condition is met, update the counter, then unconditionally jump back to the loop label. A canonical countdown example initializes R A M[counter] to ten and then decrements until zero. The important distinction from high-level languages is that there is no implicit loop frame: you must decide whether to check before or after the body. That choice creates common off-by-one behaviors. For example, checking the counter at the start prevents an extra iteration, while checking at the end will execute the body at least once. When you write a loop, name the label clearly, initialize the counter in a separate step, and use the C P U Emulator to step the first few iterations. Concrete example: a countdown from 10 to 0 uses @10, D=A, @counter, M=D, a loop label, a read of @counter into D, a conditional D;JEQ to exit, a decrement of counter, and an unconditional 0;JMP back. Misconception: you cannot rely on the PC to roll over; explicit jumps are required. Key takeaway: decide entry or exit test intentionally and verify the counter update order in the C P U Emulator.

Conditionals in Hack assembly are implemented by computing a comparison into the D register and using conditional jump instructions to skip or execute code blocks. The canonical example compares x and y by loading x into D, subtracting y, and testing the sign of D. If D is greater than zero, the program jumps to the true branch; otherwise the code falls through to the else branch. The assembly relies on the ALU to compute x minus y and the jump instructions like JGT or JEQ to inspect the result. In concrete terms, you load @x, D=M, then @y, D=D-M; if you want to execute the true branch on x > y, use D;JGT to jump to IF_TRUE. The else branch is the next instructions that store y into z, followed by an unconditional jump to END. A misconception is to assume equality and greater-than checks use the same jump—each jump condition is distinct and must match your intended logic. Practice by translating simple high-level conditionals to sequences of load, ALU, conditional jump, and store. Debug by stepping to the comparison and verifying D's numeric value before the jump. Which jump condition best captures your intended test?

Screen output on the Hack platform is achieved by writing values directly to the SCREEN memory map. The screen occupies a contiguous range of memory words; writing 0xFFFF to an address paints all pixels for that word. The standard pattern initializes an address pointer with the base SCREEN address, initializes a counter for how many words to write, then loops: check counter, write 0xFFFF to the current address, increment the address, decrement the counter, and repeat until finished. This pattern is useful for filling rectangles, clearing the screen, or painting repeated patterns. The rectangle example in the chapter shows how to prepare an address variable, a remaining-word counter, and a loop which sets M=-1 at each address. Important practical notes: compute the correct number of words for your region, and ensure the address pointer increments correctly to avoid off-by-one or writing outside the screen range. Debugging tip: use the emulator memory viewer to watch the range of SCREEN addresses while your program runs, and set a breakpoint when the counter reaches small values to confirm behavior. The key idea is that drawing is simply memory writes repeated under program control.

Reading the keyboard in Hack assembly is unusually simple: a single memory read from the keyboard address returns the ASCII code of the pressed key, or zero if no key is pressed. This makes polling loops straightforward: read the keyboard memory, test whether the value is zero, and react when it becomes nonzero. A common pattern is a tight loop that repeatedly executes @KBD, D=M and then branches depending on whether D is zero. You can then move the ASCII code to a screen register or use it in logic. A concrete program is a keyboard echo: repeatedly read KBD and write the ASCII code or an interpreted character to the screen memory so the display updates in real time as keys are pressed. Be cautious about busy-wait loops: they consume C P U cycles and block other logic; consider adding simple state checks or debouncing logic. In the C P U Emulator, press keys while running the program and watch D change from zero to the ASCII value. A common misconception is thinking keyboard reads produce character strings; they return a single code per read, and your program must decide how to display or buffer characters.

Subroutines in Hack assembly require manual management of the return address because there is no hardware call stack or automatic return mechanism. The caller is responsible for saving the return address and the callee must transfer control back to that saved address. A common software convention is to use a memory-based stack: the caller pushes the return address onto the stack, pushes any required arguments, and then jumps to the subroutine label. The subroutine runs, places its result in agreed-upon locations, pops any local values if needed, retrieves the saved return address, and jumps to it. In this chapter we do not implement a full stack mechanism, but the concept is critical: without saving the return address either by storing PC in memory or using a software stack, you cannot return reliably. A concrete way to practice is to implement a single-call routine where the caller stores the address of the next instruction into a known R A M location, jumps to the subroutine, and the subroutine jumps back to that saved address. Misconception: assuming a simple jump and then returning by another jump without a saved address will overwrite control flow. Key takeaway: always save the return point before transferring control to a subroutine.

The C P U Emulator is the primary tool for debugging Hack assembly. It lets you load an assembled program and step through instructions one at a time, inspect the PC, A and D registers, and view memory contents at any address. Use breakpoints to pause at crucial instructions, such as the conditional jump in a loop, and watch how register values and memory change across iterations. Effective debugging starts with small test cases that exercise a single loop or branch, then expands coverage. Useful techniques include tracing the first few loop iterations by hand while stepping the emulator, watching boundary values like zero and negative numbers, and monitoring memory locations used for counters and addresses. When a loop behaves incorrectly, set a breakpoint at the loop label and observe the counter before and after the decrement. For off-by-one bugs, move the decrement before the conditional check or after it to see the difference. The emulator also supports watching memory addresses so you can detect accidental writes outside intended regions. Key takeaway: combine stepping with directed tests to isolate the instruction that violates your intent.

Off-by-one errors are pervasive in assembly because you explicitly control when the counter is checked and when it is updated. When D is nonzero, write the code or a converted pixel representation to a predetermined screen address and then continue polling. Important considerations include clearing the previous display value if you want only the current key shown, and deciding whether to busy-wait or implement a simple debounce period. In the C P U Emulator you can press keys and observe the KBD memory change to nonzero and then the screen memory update immediately after. Test incrementally: first confirm that D=M reads nonzero when a key is pressed, then wire a single write to SCREEN and verify the expected memory word changes. A common mistake is assuming keyboard reads produce continuous streams; you must poll repeatedly and decide how to buffer or display sequences. This lab reinforces how a simple memory read connects directly to visible output with only a few assembly instructions.

Assembly programming relies on a small set of recurring patterns. Recognizing and composing these patterns reduces errors. The patterns are: initialization, where you set counters and pointers into memory; the loop body, which performs the work for each iteration; conditional checks that decide whether to continue or branch; and input and output actions that write to SCREEN or read KBD. Treat these as modular pieces: a program usually starts by initializing variables, then enters a loop that performs a conditional check, executes a body that may include input and output, updates state, and jumps back. Another common grouping is helper code: small subroutines that perform repeated tasks such as writing a single word to SCREEN or copying memory. In practice, keep each piece short so you can test it independently in the C P U Emulator. For example, verify your initialization alone by stepping to the first loop entry, then test the loop body with a single iteration, then validate the conditional logic. A common misconception is trying to write everything at once; instead, build and verify small pieces and combine them. Key takeaway: a reliable program comes from composing small, testable patterns and verifying each with the emulator.

Assembly programming composes high-level operations using a small set of primitives: loads and stores, ALU operations, labels, and jumps. Loops are labels plus a conditional check and an update. Conditionals compute comparisons and use specific jump instructions to pick branches. Screen input and output is achieved by writing words to the SCREEN memory range; keyboard input is a single memory read that yields the ASCII code or zero. Subroutines require you to save a return address manually, and a software stack is how nested calls are implemented in later modules. The C P U Emulator is an essential part of the workflow: step through instructions, set breakpoints at control points, and watch memory to validate logic and find off-by-one errors. Practice builds intuition: small test cases and incremental checks let you validate each pattern. These ideas form the toolbox for converting algorithms like factorial or multiplication into working Hack assembly. Which pattern will you practice first with the C P U Emulator?

Keep a short checklist when writing and testing assembly programs. First, initialize all variables and pointers explicitly. Second, choose whether your loop tests before or after the body and ensure the counter update matches that decision. Third, when implementing conditionals pick the precise jump instruction—equality, greater-than or less-than—and compute the ALU result accordingly. Fourth, for input and output remember SCREEN writes are memory writes and keyboard reads are single-code memory reads. Finally, always use the C P U Emulator to step through failing code and inspect the registers and memory cells involved in the bug. These small rules-of-thumb reduce errors and make debugging faster. As you practice, these heuristics will become habits that speed your development of correct low-level programs.
